items.title: Interior of the Earth — Layers & Discontinuities
items.body:
### Interior of the Earth

**In one line**
The Earth is built in three shells — a thin outer **crust**, a thick middle **mantle**, and a dense metallic **core** — and the surfaces where one shell changes into the next are called **discontinuities**.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims loves one-mark memory questions: which layer is molten, which discontinuity separates crust from mantle, what the core is made of. Get the order and the names right and these are free marks.

**The story**
Imagine the Earth cut like an apple. The **crust** is the thin skin — brittle and light. Under the oceans it is thin (about 5 km) and made of heavier basalt-type rock (called **SIMA**, silica + magnesium); under the continents it is thick (about 30 km) and made of lighter granite-type rock (called **SIAL**, silica + aluminium). Below the crust is the **mantle**, reaching down to about 2900 km. The top of the mantle has a soft, partly-melted zone, the **asthenosphere** (down to about 400 km), which is where magma comes from. The hard crust plus the hard top of the mantle together form the **lithosphere** (about 10–200 km thick) — this is the layer that is broken into tectonic plates. Deepest of all is the **core**, made mainly of **nickel and iron** (so it is nick-named **NIFE**). The outer core is liquid (molten, about 2200 km thick); the inner core, though hotter, is solid because the pressure is enormous (radius about 1220 km).

**Why it matters**
We cannot dig to these layers (the deepest borehole reaches only a few km), so almost everything we know comes from how **earthquake (seismic) waves** bend and stop as they pass through. The fact that one wave type cannot cross the outer core is the proof that the outer core is liquid.

**Picture it**

| Layer | What it is made of | How far down |
|---|---|---|
| Crust | SIAL (continents) / SIMA (oceans) | 5 km (ocean) to 30 km (land) |
| Mantle | Silicate rock (iron, magnesium) | Moho down to ~2900 km |
| Outer core | Nickel + iron, molten | ~2900–5150 km |
| Inner core | Nickel + iron, solid | ~5150 km to centre (~6371 km) |

The boundaries, named from top to bottom, are **Conrad** (inside the crust) · **Moho** (crust/mantle) · **Repetti** (upper/lower mantle) · **Gutenberg** (mantle/outer core) · **Lehmann** (outer/inner core).

**Terms explained**
- **Discontinuity** — a surface inside the Earth where the rock type or state suddenly changes, so seismic waves suddenly change speed.
- **Moho (Mohorovicic)** — the boundary that separates the crust from the mantle.
- **Asthenosphere** — the weak, partly-molten upper-mantle layer that feeds volcanoes.
- **NIFE** — nickel (Ni) + ferrum/iron (Fe), the make-up of the core.

**Don't confuse**
- **Lithosphere vs asthenosphere**: lithosphere = the rigid plate (crust + hard upper mantle); asthenosphere = the soft layer it floats on.
- **Moho vs Gutenberg**: Moho = crust/mantle (near the top); Gutenberg = mantle/outer core (much deeper).
- **Outer vs inner core**: outer is liquid, inner is solid — even though the inner core is hotter, pressure keeps it solid.

**Remember it**
Discontinuities top-down read as **'Commander Mohit is ReGuLar'** = Conrad, Moho, Repetti, Gutenberg, Lehmann.

**TL;DR**
- Three shells: crust, mantle (to ~2900 km), core (NIFE = nickel + iron).
- Oceanic crust = basaltic, denser, younger, ~5 km; continental crust = granitic, thicker, older, ~30 km.
- Moho separates crust from mantle; Gutenberg separates mantle from outer core.
- Outer core molten, inner core solid; asthenosphere is the source of magma.
- Oxygen = most abundant element in the crust; aluminium = most abundant metal in the crust; iron = most abundant metal in the whole Earth.

Outer core is molten, inner core is solid; the asthenosphere is the source of magma.
Oxygen is the most abundant crustal element; iron is the most abundant metal in the whole Earth.

items.title: From Continental Drift to Plate Tectonics
items.body:
### From Continental Drift to Plate Tectonics

**In one line**
The idea that today's continents were once joined and have slowly drifted apart grew, over fifty years, into **plate tectonics** — the master theory that the Earth's hard outer shell is broken into moving plates.

**Why it is asked**
Examiners test who proposed what (Wegener, Holmes, Hess), the names Pangaea/Panthalassa/Tethys, the list of major plates, and the three boundary types with their examples.

**The story**
In **1912** the German meteorologist **Alfred Wegener** noticed that the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like jigsaw pieces. He proposed that all land once formed a single supercontinent, **Pangaea** ('all earth'), surrounded by one ocean, **Panthalassa**. A sea called **Tethys** later split Pangaea into a northern mass, **Laurasia**, and a southern mass, **Gondwanaland**; drifting began roughly 200 million years ago. Wegener's problem was *force*: the pushes he suggested (buoyancy, tides, gravity) were far too weak to shove continents. The missing engine came from **Arthur Holmes** in the 1930s, who argued that heat from **radioactive decay** stirs the mantle in slow **convection currents**. **Harry Hess** then showed how it works at the sea floor: molten rock rises at mid-ocean ridges, hardens into new crust, and pushes the older crust sideways — **sea-floor spreading**. The clinching proof was **palaeomagnetism**: strips of sea-floor rock record the Earth's magnetic field flipping, and the pattern is a mirror image on both sides of a ridge. Finally **McKenzie and Parker (1967)** and **Morgan (1968)** tied it together as **plate tectonics**.

**Why it matters**
Plate tectonics explains, with one idea, where mountains rise, where oceans open, and why earthquakes and volcanoes cluster along certain lines — so it underlies almost every other geography topic.

**Picture it**

| Boundary | Plates do what | Result | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Divergent (constructive) | move apart | new crust, ridges, rifts | Mid-ocean ridge, East African Rift |
| Convergent (destructive) | push together | folding, trenches, subduction | Himalayas, ocean trenches |
| Transform | slide past | crust neither made nor destroyed | San Andreas Fault |

The **seven major plates** are Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Antarctic and Indo-Australian; smaller ones include Nazca, Cocos, Arabian, Philippine, Caribbean and Juan de Fuca.

**Terms explained**
- **Pangaea / Panthalassa** — the single ancient supercontinent and the single ocean around it.
- **Palaeomagnetism** — the record of past magnetic-field directions frozen into rock, used to prove spreading.
- **Subduction** — one plate sliding down beneath another at a convergent boundary.

**Divergence in an ocean vs on a continent**
When plates pull apart under an **ocean**, the gap fills with new crust and forms a **mid-ocean ridge** (Mid-Atlantic Ridge). When a **continent** itself is being pulled apart, its middle drops down between faults into a **rift valley** — the **East African Rift Valley** is the classic example.

**Don't confuse**
- **Continental drift vs plate tectonics**: drift (Wegener) said continents move but could not say how; plate tectonics supplies the mechanism (convection + spreading).
- **Divergent vs convergent**: divergent builds new crust (ridge); convergent destroys/crumples crust (mountain or trench).
- **Holmes vs Hess**: Holmes = mantle convection idea; Hess = sea-floor spreading.

**Remember it**
Boundary outcomes: **Divergent = build** (ridge), **Convergent = crush** (mountain/trench), **Transform = slide** (fault).

**The Indian Plate**
India broke off Gondwanaland, drifted north across the Tethys Sea, and **collided with Asia about 40–50 million years ago**, crumpling sediments into the **Himalayas** — which are still rising as India keeps pushing. The same northward journey triggered the **Deccan Trap** flood-basalt eruptions about 60 million years ago.

**TL;DR**
- Wegener (1912) proposed Continental Drift — Pangaea + Panthalassa, split by Tethys into Laurasia and Gondwanaland.
- Drift evidence: coastline fit, Glossopteris flora, Mesosaurus fossils, tillite and placer deposits.
- Harry Hess proposed sea-floor spreading; palaeomagnetism is its key proof; Holmes proposed mantle convection.
- Seven major plates; boundaries are divergent (ridges), convergent (trenches/mountains) or transform (San Andreas Fault).
- The Indian plate collided with Asia 40–50 mya, uplifting the still-rising Himalayas and forming the Deccan Traps.

items.title: Earthquakes — Waves, Measurement & Distribution
items.body:
### Earthquakes

**In one line**
An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground when stored stress in the rocks is released, sending out **seismic waves** that we record and measure.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims asks the focus-vs-epicentre difference, which wave proves the liquid outer core, the Richter energy jump, and where quakes concentrate (Ring of Fire, India's Zone V).

**The story**
Rocks under stress finally snap along a fault. The point inside the Earth where the energy is first released is the **focus** (or **hypocentre**); the point on the surface straight above it is the **epicentre**, which shakes first and hardest. Small quakes before the main shock are **foreshocks**, those after are **aftershocks**, and a cluster of small quakes with no single main shock is a **swarm**. Quakes are grouped by how deep the focus is: **shallow** (0–70 km) release about 70–85% of all energy and do the most damage, **intermediate** (70–300 km) and **deep** (300–700 km). Most quakes are **tectonic** (fault slip); some are **volcanic**; and some are **human-induced** — for example the 1967 **Koynanagar** quake linked to a reservoir.

**Why it matters**
Seismic waves are our main X-ray of the planet: because **S-waves cannot pass through liquid**, their absence beyond a certain depth is the proof that the outer core is molten.

**Picture it**

| Wave | Nature | Travels through | Speed / Damage |
|---|---|---|---|
| P (primary) | push-pull (longitudinal) | solid, liquid, gas | Fastest, arrives first, least damage |
| S (secondary) | shake (transverse) | solids only | Medium; blocked by liquid (proves molten outer core) |
| L (surface) | along the surface | the surface | Slowest, arrives last, most damage |

**Terms explained**
- **Focus / epicentre** — focus = underground release point; epicentre = the surface point directly above it.
- **Richter scale** — a number for the **energy** released; **Mercalli scale** — a number for the **intensity** (observed effects/damage).
- **Ring of Fire** — the earthquake-and-volcano belt around the rim of the Pacific Ocean.

**Richter energy — worked out**
The Richter scale is **logarithmic**: each whole step is about **32 times** more energy. So from magnitude 5.0 to 7.0 is two steps, that is 32 × 32 = **1,024 ≈ 1,000 times** more energy. (One step = ~32×; two steps = ~1,000×.)

**Don't confuse**
- **Richter vs Mercalli**: Richter = energy (one number for the quake); Mercalli = intensity (varies from place to place).
- **Focus vs epicentre**: focus is below ground, epicentre is on the surface.
- **P-wave vs S-wave**: both are body waves, but only S-waves are stopped by liquids.

**Remember it**
Waves are **recorded** fastest-to-slowest as P → S → L; their **destructiveness** is the reverse, L > S > P.

**Distribution**
The **Circum-Pacific Belt (Ring of Fire)** has about 68% of all quakes; the **Alpine–Himalayan belt** about 15% of the energy; mid-ocean ridges make up the rest. India is split into **five seismic zones (II–V)**; **Zone V** is highest risk (NE India, the Himalayas, Kutch, Andaman–Nicobar), and roughly 59% of India's area faces moderate-to-severe risk.

**TL;DR**
- Focus = underground release point; epicentre = surface point above it; shallow quakes are the most destructive.
- P-waves travel through everything and are fastest; S-waves cannot pass liquids (proving a molten outer core).
- Surface (L) waves are slowest but most destructive.
- Richter: one step ≈ 32× energy, two steps ≈ 1,000×; Mercalli measures intensity/effects.
- Ring of Fire ≈ 68% of earthquakes; Zone V is India's highest seismic-risk zone.

items.title: Volcanoes & Rocks
items.body:
### Volcanoes & Rocks

**In one line**
Volcanoes are openings through which molten rock reaches the surface, and the three great families of rock — **igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic** — are the materials the crust is built from and recycled through.

**Why it is asked**
Typical questions: match a volcano type to an example, match an intrusive landform to its shape, and match an original rock to what it turns into (limestone → marble, etc.).

**The story**
How a volcano looks depends on how runny its lava is. **Thin, fluid basaltic lava** flows far and builds broad, gently sloping **shield volcanoes** (Mauna Loa) — big but gentle. **Thick, sticky lava** traps gas and erupts violently, piling up steep **composite volcanoes (stratovolcanoes)** of alternating lava and ash (Fuji, Vesuvius, Etna) along the Ring of Fire. A giant eruption can empty the magma chamber so the top collapses into a **caldera** (Yellowstone; Crater Lake) — the most explosive type. Where fluid lava pours out of long cracks over huge areas it forms **flood basalts** (the **Deccan Traps**). Magma that cools *underground* makes **intrusive** landforms: a **batholith** (the largest, deep granite body), a **dyke** (a thin vertical sheet cutting across layers), a **sill** (a horizontal sheet between layers) and a **laccolith** (a lens- or dome-shaped intrusion that bulges the overlying rock layers upward).

**Why it matters**
Rock type decides what minerals, soils and fossils a region has — the practical reason this topic links to resources and to palaeontology.

**Picture it**

| Rock group | How it forms | Clue | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Igneous (primary) | magma/lava cools | no fossils | granite (underground), basalt (surface) |
| Sedimentary | sediments compacted | layers + fossils | sandstone, shale, limestone, coal |
| Metamorphic | heat + pressure change old rock | banded/foliated | gneiss, slate, schist, marble, quartzite |

Metamorphism pairs: limestone → marble · sandstone → quartzite · coal → graphite/anthracite · granite → gneiss · clay/shale → slate/schist.

**Terms explained**
- **Igneous ('fire-formed')** — made by cooling of magma (underground) or lava (surface); called *primary* because the other two groups ultimately come from it.
- **Metamorphism** — the re-cooking of an existing rock by heat and pressure into a new, harder rock without melting it.
- **Rock cycle** — the endless loop in which any rock type can, over time, become any other (subduction even remelts crust back into magma).

**Don't confuse**
- **Shield vs composite**: shield = thin lava, gentle, huge, calm; composite = thick lava, steep, violent.
- **Dyke vs sill**: dyke is vertical (cuts across layers); sill is horizontal (lies along layers).
- **Basalt is igneous, not metamorphic** — a common trap.

**Remember it**
Explosivity rises with lava thickness: **Shield (thin/calm) < Composite < Caldera (thick/violent)**.

**TL;DR**
- Shield (fluid basalt, gentle, Mauna Loa) vs composite (viscous, steep, Fuji) vs caldera (most explosive).
- Deccan Traps are a flood-basalt province of highly fluid lava.
- Intrusive landforms: batholith (largest), dyke (vertical), sill (horizontal), laccolith (dome).
- Three rock groups: igneous (primary, no fossils), sedimentary (layered/fossil-bearing), metamorphic (foliated).
- Metamorphism: limestone→marble, sandstone→quartzite, coal→graphite, granite→gneiss; feldspar and quartz are the commonest rock-forming minerals.

items.title: Geological Time Scale & Earth-shaping Forces
items.body:
### Geological Time Scale & Earth-shaping Forces

**In one line**
The **geological time scale** is the calendar of the Earth's 4.6-billion-year history, and the surface we see is the result of two opposite sets of forces — **endogenic** (building up) and **exogenic** (wearing down).

**Why it is asked**
Prelims asks the time-scale order (Eon > Era > Period > Epoch), when the dinosaurs died out, and the endogenic-vs-exogenic distinction with terms like orogeny and denudation.

**The story**
Earth is about **4.6 billion years** old, and its history is divided, largest to smallest, into **Eon > Era > Period > Epoch**. Key markers: the **Cambrian** (~505–570 million years ago) teemed with sea invertebrates but had no land life; the **Carboniferous** laid down the great coal beds and saw the first reptiles; the **Permian** ended in a mass extinction; the **Jurassic** was the Age of Dinosaurs; the **Cretaceous** closed with the dinosaurs' extinction about 65 million years ago; and in the **Quaternary**, humans appear (Pleistocene) and modern humans in the **Holocene**. Meanwhile two force families fight over the surface. **Endogenic (internal) forces**, powered by internal heat (mostly radioactive decay) and convection, *build up* relief. They act slowly as **diastrophism** — **epeirogeny** (broad up-and-down warping of whole continents) and **orogeny** (mountain-building by folding and faulting) — and suddenly as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. **Exogenic (external) forces**, powered by the **Sun**, *wear down* relief through **denudation** = **weathering** + **erosion**.

**Why it matters**
Almost every landform is a snapshot of this tug-of-war: uplift raises the land, the Sun-driven agents cut it back down, and the balance between them sets the scenery.

**Picture it**

| Force family | Powered by | What it does | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Endogenic (internal) | internal heat, convection | builds up | mountains, plateaus, earthquakes, volcanoes |
| Exogenic (external) | solar energy | wears down | weathering, river/glacier/wind erosion |

**Terms explained**
- **Weathering** — breaking rock *in place* (physical: frost, exfoliation, salt; chemical: carbonation, hydration, hydrolysis, oxidation; biological).
- **Erosion** — the *removal and carrying away* of the broken debris by water, wind, ice or waves.
- **Diastrophism** — slow bending/raising of the crust; its two kinds are epeirogeny (broad) and orogeny (mountain-building).
- **Mountain types** — fold, block (faulting), volcanic and residual (an erosional leftover).

**The four mountain types, with examples**

| Type | How it forms | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Fold | plates press rock layers into folds | Himalayas and the Alps |
| Block | a block (horst) is pushed up between two faults | Black Forest and Vosges, either side of the Rhine rift valley |
| Volcanic | built up from erupted lava and ash | Mount Kilimanjaro and Fujiyama |
| Residual (relict) | an old range worn down by erosion | Aravalli Range (India) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Weathering vs erosion**: weathering breaks rock on the spot; erosion then transports it. (Weathering + erosion = denudation.)
- **Epeirogeny vs orogeny**: epeirogeny = gentle, continent-wide uplift/warping; orogeny = localised mountain-building.
- **Endogenic vs exogenic**: internal heat builds up; solar energy wears down.

**Remember it**
**ENDO**genic = **EN**ergy from **D**eep (internal, builds up); **EXO**genic = **EX**ternal Sun (wears down). W. M. Davis founded the science of geomorphology.

**TL;DR**
- Time-scale hierarchy: Eon > Era > Period > Epoch; Earth is ~4.6 billion years old.
- Dinosaurs dominated in the Jurassic and went extinct at the end of the Cretaceous (~65 mya).
- Endogenic forces (internal heat) build up the surface; exogenic forces (solar energy) wear it down.
- Diastrophism = epeirogeny (broad uplift) + orogeny (mountain building by folding/faulting).
- Denudation = weathering (in-situ breakdown) + erosion (removal); mountain types are fold, block, volcanic and residual.

items.title: Landforms of External Agents (River, Glacier, Wind, Karst, Sea)
items.body:
### Landforms of External Agents

**In one line**
Each external agent — **river, glacier, wind, groundwater (karst) and sea** — carves its own signature set of landforms, first by eroding and later by depositing the debris.

**Why it is asked**
These are classic match-the-landform-to-the-agent questions: oxbow lake (river), cirque/fjord (glacier), barchan (wind), stalactite/sinkhole (karst), sea stack/tombolo (sea).

**The story**
A **river** changes job along its course. In its **youth** it cuts down hard, making **V-shaped valleys, gorges, canyons, waterfalls and potholes**. In **maturity** it swings sideways into **meanders**, and a cut-off meander becomes an **oxbow lake** (Kanwar Lake, Bihar — India's largest). In **old age** it drops its load as **deltas, natural levees, alluvial fans and braided channels** (Majuli, Assam — the world's largest river island). A **glacier** scoops out **cirques** (which later hold a **tarn** lake), **U-shaped troughs**, **hanging valleys**, knife-edge **aretes**, pyramid **horns** and drowned **fjords**; it dumps **moraines, eskers, drumlins, kettle holes and outwash plains** (Siachen in the Karakoram is India's largest glacier). **Wind** in deserts carves **yardangs, zeugen, inselbergs, mushroom rocks and deflation basins**, and builds **sand dunes** (the crescent **barchan**, linear **seif**, **star** and **parabolic**) plus **loess** — fertile wind-blown silt. **Groundwater** dissolving limestone makes **karst**: **sinkholes, dolines, uvalas, poljes, caves**, and the dripstone pair **stalactites** (hang from the ceiling) and **stalagmites** (grow up from the floor). The **sea** erodes **wave-cut platforms, sea caves, arches and stacks**, and deposits **beaches, bars, lagoons, spits, hooks and tombolos** (a bar linking an island to the mainland).

**Why it matters**
Recognising the agent from the landform (and vice versa) is exactly what one-mark map/photo questions test.

**Picture it**

| Agent | Erosional landforms | Depositional landforms |
|---|---|---|
| River | V-valley, gorge, waterfall, pothole | meander, oxbow lake, delta, levee, alluvial fan |
| Glacier | cirque, U-valley, arete, horn, fjord | moraine, esker, drumlin, kettle, outwash plain |
| Wind | yardang, zeugen, inselberg, mushroom rock | barchan/seif dunes, ripple marks, loess |
| Karst | sinkhole, doline, polje, cave | stalactite, stalagmite, pillar |
| Sea | wave-cut platform, sea cave, arch, stack | beach, bar, lagoon, spit, tombolo |

**What the glacial and desert names mean**
- **Cirque** — an armchair-shaped hollow at a glacier's head; it may hold a small **tarn** lake.
- **Arete** — a steep-sided, sharp (knife-edge) ridge between two glacial valleys.
- **Esker** — a long, winding ridge of glacial debris (sand and gravel) on a till plain.
- **Fjord** — a steep-sided, narrow glacial valley drowned by the sea at the coast (Norway).
- **Barchan** — a crescent-shaped sand dune whose horns point downwind.
- **Yardang** — a streamlined rock ridge carved by wind, lying parallel to the prevailing wind.
- **Playa** — a temporary, shallow salt lake on the floor of a desert basin (a bolson).

**Terms explained**
- **Delta** — the fan of sediment at a river mouth; types are arcuate (Ganga, Nile), bird's-foot (Mississippi), cuspate (Tiber) and estuarine (Narmada, Tapi).
- **Loess** — very fine wind-blown silt that forms deep, fertile soils (e.g. the Hwang-Ho basin).
- **Karst** — scenery made by rainwater dissolving limestone; named after the Karst region in the Balkans.

**Karst and sea words, explained**
- **Sinkhole** — a funnel-shaped hollow on limestone (karst) ground, made when rock dissolves and the surface sinks.
- **Stalactite / stalagmite** — limestone 'icicles' in karst caves, hanging from the ceiling / rising from the floor.
- **Sea stack** — a pillar of rock left standing in the sea when a sea arch collapses (marine erosion).
- **Tombolo** — a sand or shingle bar that joins an island to the mainland (marine deposition).

**Don't confuse**
- **Stalactite vs stalagmite**: stalaCtite hangs from the Ceiling; stalaGmite grows from the Ground.
- **Barchan vs parabolic dune**: barchan horns point downwind; parabolic (vegetation-anchored) horns point upwind.
- **Fjord vs ria**: both are drowned valleys, but a fjord is a drowned *glacial* valley; a ria is a drowned *river* valley.

**Remember it**
Dripstone: **stalaCtite = Ceiling, stalaGmite = Ground**.

**TL;DR**
- Fluvial: V-valley/gorge/waterfall (youth) → meander/oxbow lake (maturity) → delta/levee (old age).
- Delta types: arcuate (Ganga), bird's-foot (Mississippi), cuspate (Tiber), estuarine (Narmada/Tapi).
- Glacial erosional: cirque, U-valley, arete, horn, fjord; depositional: moraine, esker, drumlin.
- Barchan dunes are crescent-shaped with tips pointing downwind; loess is fertile wind-blown silt.
- Karst: sinkholes, poljes, caves, stalactites (ceiling) and stalagmites (floor); Marine: wave-cut platform, sea arch, stack (erosional); spit, lagoon, tombolo (depositional).

items.title: Indian Rock Systems, Minerals, Shale Gas & Barren Island
items.body:
### Indian Rock Systems, Minerals, Shale Gas & Barren Island

**In one line**
India's rocks are grouped by age into **systems** (Dharwar, Cuddapah, Gondwana, Tertiary), and each system is linked to particular minerals — a pairing the exam loves to test, alongside India's only active volcano, **Barren Island**.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims (UPSC 2013/2015/2018 style) repeatedly pairs a rock system with its mineral, asks where shale gas occurs, and tests whether Barren Island is active or dormant.

**The story**
The **Dharwar system** is the **oldest** group of metamorphosed sediments and is rich in **metallic minerals** — iron, manganese, gold (Kolar) and copper — but it has **no petroleum**. The **Cuddapah system** (Proterozoic) carries iron, manganese, limestone, asbestos and barytes. The **Gondwana system** (Carboniferous–Permian) is India's coal treasury, holding about **98% of the country's coal**, plus sandstone. **Petroleum** instead comes from the much younger **Tertiary** rocks, which also hold the lignite (younger coal) of the north-east. Separately, **Kodarma in Jharkhand** is India's **mica** belt. **Shale gas** — natural gas locked inside fine-grained **sedimentary shale** and freed by hydraulic fracturing — is found in the **Cambay, Krishna-Godavari and Cauvery** basins (also Gondwana, Assam-Arakan and Indo-Gangetic). Finally, **Barren Island**, in the **Andaman Sea**, is **India's only active volcano**; it has erupted repeatedly **after 1991** (for example in 2017), so it is **not** dormant, while nearby **Narcondam** is regarded as dormant.

**Why it matters**
This note turns a dry list into exam-ready pairs and corrects two favourite traps (Dharwar ≠ oil; Barren Island ≠ dormant).

**Picture it**

| System | Age | Characteristic minerals |
|---|---|---|
| Dharwar | oldest metamorphosed sediments | iron, manganese, gold (Kolar), copper |
| Cuddapah | Proterozoic | iron, manganese, limestone, asbestos, barytes |
| Gondwana | Carboniferous–Permian | coal (~98% of India's coal), sandstone |
| Tertiary | Cenozoic | petroleum, younger (lignite) coal in NE India |

**Terms explained**
- **Rock system** — a body of rock formed during a particular span of geological time.
- **Shale gas** — natural gas trapped in shale (a fine-grained sedimentary rock), extracted by hydraulic fracturing ('fracking').
- **Active vs dormant volcano** — active = has erupted in recent history; dormant = quiet now but could erupt again.

**Don't confuse**
- **Dharwar vs Tertiary**: metals (and gold) come from Dharwar; **petroleum comes from Tertiary**, not Dharwar.
- **Coal source**: ~98% of India's coal is **Gondwana**, not Tertiary (Tertiary gives only the younger lignite).
- **Barren vs Narcondam**: Barren Island is active; Narcondam is dormant — and Barren Island is in the Andaman group, not near Great Nicobar.

**Remember it**
**Coal = Gondwana, Oil = Tertiary, Metals = Dharwar, Mica = Kodarma.**

**TL;DR**
- Dharwar system = oldest metamorphosed rocks, rich in metallic minerals (iron, manganese, gold) — NOT petroleum.
- Gondwana rocks hold ~98% of India's coal; petroleum comes from Tertiary rocks; Kodarma (Jharkhand) is the mica belt.
- Shale gas occurs in the Cambay, Krishna-Godavari and Cauvery sedimentary basins.
- Barren Island (Andaman Sea) is India's only active volcano and has erupted after 1991 (not dormant).
- Narcondam is India's other volcanic island and is regarded as dormant.

items.title: Interior of the Earth — Numbers, Densities & Shadow Zones
items.body:
### The interior in numbers

**In one line**
Each layer of the Earth has its own thickness, density and temperature, and density rises steadily from about **2.7 g/cm³** in the crust to about **13 g/cm³** in the inner core.

**The story**
Nobody has drilled through the crust — the deepest hole, the **Kola Superdeep Borehole** in Russia, reached only about **12 km**. So we learn about the interior from **direct sources** (mines, boreholes, volcanic lava) and, far more, from **indirect sources**: rising temperature and pressure with depth, **meteorites** (which share the Earth's material), gravity and magnetic surveys, and above all **seismic waves**. The Earth's mean radius is about **6,371 km**.

**Crust: oceanic vs continental**

| | Oceanic crust | Continental crust |
|---|---|---|
| Rock | basaltic | granitic |
| Density | about 3.0 g/cm³ | about 2.7 g/cm³ |
| Mean thickness | about 5 km | about 30 km |
| Age | younger | older |

The upper crust is **SiAl** (silica + aluminium, density **2.7**); the lower crust is **SiMa** (silica + magnesium, density **3.0**). The **Conrad discontinuity** separates them.

**Mantle and core**

| Layer | Key numbers and facts |
|---|---|
| Asthenosphere | upper mantle down to about **400 km**; "astheno" means **weak**; the main source of **magma** |
| Lithosphere | crust + uppermost mantle, **10–200 km** thick |
| Lower mantle | below the asthenosphere, in a **solid** state |
| Mantle as a whole | Moho to about **2,900 km**; silicate minerals rich in iron and magnesium; density **3.3 to 5.7 g/cm³** |
| Outer core | molten iron–nickel, about **2,200 km** thick, density **9.9–12.2 g/cm³**, about **4,000–6,000°C** |
| Inner core | solid iron–nickel, about **1,220 km** (radius), density **12.6–13.0 g/cm³**, about **5,400°C** |

**Abundant elements**: **oxygen** is the most abundant element in the crust; **aluminium** the most abundant metal in the crust; **iron** the most abundant metal in the whole Earth. (Standard order of crustal elements: oxygen, silicon, aluminium, iron.)

**Shadow zones**
Seen from an earthquake's epicentre, **P-waves** are not recorded between about **103° and 142°** of arc — the **P-wave shadow zone**, caused by refraction at the core. **S-waves** are not recorded at all beyond about **103°**, because they cannot cross the liquid outer core. So the S-wave shadow zone is much larger than the P-wave one.

**Terms explained**
- **Shadow zone** — a belt of the Earth's surface where a given seismic wave does not arrive.
- **Meteorite evidence** — meteorites are made of material similar to the Earth's, so they hint at its make-up.

**Don't confuse**
SiAl (upper, 2.7) vs SiMa (lower, 3.0). The P-wave shadow is a ring (103°–142°); the S-wave shadow is everything beyond 103°.

**TL;DR**
- Oceanic crust: basaltic, 3.0 g/cm³, ~5 km, younger; continental: granitic, 2.7 g/cm³, ~30 km, older.
- Asthenosphere to ~400 km (weak, magma source); lithosphere 10–200 km; mantle density 3.3–5.7.
- Outer core ~2,200 km thick, molten, 4,000–6,000°C; inner core ~1,220 km, solid, ~5,400°C, density up to 13.0.
- P-wave shadow 103°–142°; S-waves absent beyond 103°; Kola borehole ~12 km deep.
keyPoints: Oceanic crust density ~3.0 g/cm³ (basalt, ~5 km); continental ~2.7 g/cm³ (granite, ~30 km).
SiAl (upper crust, 2.7) and SiMa (lower crust, 3.0) are separated by the Conrad discontinuity.
Asthenosphere ("weak") extends to ~400 km; lithosphere is 10–200 km thick; lower mantle is solid.
Mantle density rises from 3.3 to 5.7 g/cm³; outer core 9.9–12.2; inner core 12.6–13.0.
Outer core ~2,200 km thick at 4,000–6,000°C; inner core ~1,220 km at ~5,400°C.
P-wave shadow zone 103°–142°; S-wave shadow zone beyond 103°.
Kola Superdeep Borehole (~12 km) is the deepest drilling; meteorites are an indirect source.

items.title: Wegener's Evidence, the Drift Debate & the Plates in Detail
items.body:
### Proving that continents move

**In one line**
Wegener backed continental drift with **six kinds of evidence**; its weakness was the force, which Holmes's convection and Hess's sea-floor spreading later supplied; plate tectonics then named seven major and many minor plates.

**The story**
Alfred Wegener first presented continental drift in **1912**; the 1922 edition of his book (our source gives **1922**) made it famous. He imagined drift beginning about **200 million years** ago, pushed by a **pole-fleeing force** (from the centrifugal force of rotation) and **tidal force** (pulling westward). Critics replied that these forces were far too weak to move continents.

**Wegener's evidence**

| Evidence | Example |
|---|---|
| Jig-saw fit (apparent affinity) | **Brazil** fits into the **Gulf of Guinea** (Africa); Greenland fits Ellesmere and Baffin islands; the **Caledonian and Hercynian** mountains of Europe continue in the **Appalachians** |
| Botanical | **Glossopteris** flora in India, Australia, South Africa, Falklands and Antarctica — all once **Gondwana** |
| Fossils | **Lemurs** in India, Madagascar and Africa (the imagined land "**Lemuria**"); **Mesosaurus**, a small brackish-water reptile, found only in **South Africa and Brazil**, now **4,800 km** apart |
| Tillite | glacial sediments of the **Gondwana** system in India, Africa, Falklands, Madagascar, Antarctica and Australia |
| Placer gold | rich gold placers in **West Africa** with no source rock there — derived from the **Brazil plateau** |
| Rocks of same age | **2,000-million-year**-old rock belts of coastal Brazil match those of western Africa |

**Recap** — Pangaea was surrounded by a single ocean, **Panthalassa**; the **Tethys Sea** divided Pangaea into **Laurasia** in the north and **Gondwanaland** in the south.

**Drawbacks** — it could not explain why drift began only in the **Mesozoic**, had no explanation of ocean spreading, and its forces were too weak.

**Plate tectonics — the plates**
The theory came from **McKenzie and Parker (1967)**, outlined by **Morgan (1968)**: the lithosphere is broken into plates **floating on the asthenosphere**, moved by mantle convection.

| Major plates (7) | Minor plates (examples) |
|---|---|
| Antarctica and surrounding oceanic plate; North American; South American; Pacific; India–Australia–New Zealand; Africa with the eastern Atlantic floor; Eurasia and adjacent oceanic plate | **Cocos** (Central America–Pacific), **Nazca** (South America–Pacific), **Arabian** (Saudi Arabia), **Philippine** (Asia–Pacific), **Caroline** (north of New Guinea), **Fuji** (north-east of Australia), Turkish, Aegean, **Caribbean**, **Juan de Fuca** (Pacific–North America), Iranian |

**Evidence for plate tectonics**: paleomagnetism (paleomagnetic stripes across ridges), **older rocks on continents and younger rocks on the ocean floor**, gravity anomalies, and the belts of earthquakes and volcanoes.

**Indian Plate timeline**
- Until about **225 million years ago** India was a large island off Australia, separated from Asia by the Tethys.
- Northward journey began about **200 million years ago**; about **140 million years ago** it lay far south, in the Southern Hemisphere.
- About **60 million years ago** the **Deccan Trap** lava outpouring began; collision with Asia came **40–50 million years ago**.

**PYQ angle (UPSC 2014)**: both **continental drift** and **glacial cycles** influenced the evolution of organisms.

**Don't confuse**
Lemuria (lemurs) vs Mesosaurus (South Africa–Brazil). Cocos and Nazca are minor plates — not among the seven major plates.

**TL;DR**
- Drift: 1912 (book editions to 1922); forces = pole-fleeing + tidal; too weak.
- Evidence: Brazil–Gulf of Guinea fit, Glossopteris, Lemurs, Mesosaurus (4,800 km apart), tillite, placer gold, 2,000-million-year rocks.
- Plate tectonics: McKenzie and Parker 1967, Morgan 1968; plates float on the asthenosphere.
- Minor plates: Cocos, Nazca, Arabian, Philippine, Caroline, Fuji, Caribbean, Juan de Fuca, Turkish, Aegean, Iranian.
keyPoints: Wegener: drift proposed 1912 (source cites 1922); pole-fleeing and tidal forces; drift began ~200 million years ago.
Jig-saw fit: Brazil fits the Gulf of Guinea; Caledonian/Hercynian mountains continue in the Appalachians.
Glossopteris flora links India, Australia, South Africa, Falklands and Antarctica (Gondwana).
Mesosaurus fossils occur only in South Africa and Brazil, now 4,800 km apart; lemurs suggested Lemuria.
Placer gold of West Africa came from the Brazil plateau; tillite is glacial sedimentary rock.
Drawback: could not explain why drift began only in the Mesozoic.
Plate tectonics: McKenzie and Parker (1967), Morgan (1968).
Minor plates include Cocos, Nazca, Arabian, Philippine, Caroline, Fuji, Caribbean and Juan de Fuca.
Indian Plate: separated by Tethys till ~225 mya; journey from ~200 mya; Deccan lava ~60 mya; collision 40–50 mya.

items.title: Earthquakes — Causes, Energy Shares, Magnitude Classes & Great Quakes
items.body:
### Earthquakes in more detail

**In one line**
Most earthquakes come from fault slip, but volcanoes, mines and reservoirs also trigger them; shallow quakes release most energy; and the magnitude scale runs from "micro" to "great" with famous examples at each level.

**The story**
Rock layers along a **fault** are pushed in opposite directions but held by **friction**; when the stress beats the friction they jerk, sending **seismic waves** in all directions. Larger faulted areas give larger magnitudes. **Volcanic** quakes are usually weaker and more local. **Human-induced** quakes come from mining, large petroleum extraction, nuclear tests and artificial lakes. In **reservoir-induced seismicity** the weight of water in a deep reservoir alters stress on an old fault and seeping water lubricates it — the **1967 Koynanagar earthquake (magnitude 6.3)** near the **Koyna Dam** in **Maharashtra** killed more than 150 people.

**Depth and energy**

| Class | Depth of focus | Share of total earthquake energy |
|---|---|---|
| Shallow | 0–70 km | about 70–85% |
| Intermediate | 70–300 km | about 12–15% |
| Deep | 300–700 km | about 3–5% |

Depth matters: on **24 August 2016** a shallow (about 10 km) magnitude 6.2 quake in **central Italy** killed about 300 people, while a deeper (84 km) 6.8 quake in **Myanmar** that day killed very few.

**The waves — extra names and numbers**
- **P-waves** are also called **compressional** or **pressure** waves; they travel at about **5–8 km/s** and move faster in solids than liquids than gases.
- **S-waves** are also called **shear** or **distortional** waves; slightly more destructive than P-waves.
- **Surface (L) waves** are **low-frequency**, die out with depth, but lose energy slowly with distance — hence most damage. A **seismograph** records all three.

**Measuring**
**Charles F. Richter** devised the Richter scale in the **1930s**. It works best for regional quakes up to about magnitude 5; the **moment magnitude scale** is better for large quakes. The **Mercalli scale** (12 levels, I–XII) rates intensity from observed damage.

| Magnitude | Class | Frequency | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0–1.9 | Micro | several million a year | — |
| 2.0–2.9 | Minor | over one million a year | — |
| 4.0–4.9 | Light | 10,000–15,000 a year | — |
| 5.0–5.9 | Moderate | 1,000–1,500 a year | — |
| 6.0–6.9 | Strong | 100–150 a year | 2011 Christchurch (6.2) |
| 7.0–7.9 | Major | 10–20 a year | 1819 **Rann of Kutch**; **2001 Gujarat (7.7)** |
| 8.0–8.9 | Great | about one a year | **1950 Assam–Tibet (8.6)**; 2008 Sichuan; 2010 Chile (8.8) |
| 9.0+ | — | one per 10–50 years | **1960 Valdivia, Chile (9.4–9.6, largest recorded)**; 1964 Alaska (9.2); **2004 Indian Ocean (9.1–9.3)**; 2011 Tohoku, Japan (9.1) |

**Belts** — besides the Ring of Fire and the **Alpine belt** (which runs from Mexico across the Atlantic, the Mediterranean and the Alpine–Caucasus ranges to the Himalayas), quakes follow the mid-ocean ridges and the **East African rift valleys**.

**Seismic zones of India** — the BIS map has four zones (II–V). **Zone V** is the highest-risk seismic zone, covering NE India, the Himalayas, Kutch and the Andaman–Nicobar Islands.

**The AP angle**
Most of Andhra Pradesh lies in the lower-risk **Zones II and III**; the Krishna–Godavari coastal belt and the Ongole region are in **Zone III**. The **2004 Indian Ocean tsunami** struck the AP coast.

**Don't confuse**
Koyna (reservoir-induced, Maharashtra) vs Latur 1993 (stable-continent quake). Richter = energy; Mercalli = intensity.

**TL;DR**
- Causes: faults (most), volcanoes, human activity, reservoirs (Koyna 1967, 6.3).
- Shallow 0–70 km (70–85% energy), intermediate 70–300 km (12–15%), deep 300–700 km (3–5%).
- P-waves 5–8 km/s; Richter 1930s; moment magnitude for big quakes; Mercalli I–XII.
- Largest recorded: Valdivia 1960 (9.4–9.6); India: 1950 Assam–Tibet 8.6, 2001 Gujarat 7.7.
keyPoints: Reservoir-induced seismicity: 1967 Koynanagar earthquake (6.3) near Koyna Dam, Maharashtra.
Human-induced quakes: mining, petroleum extraction, artificial lakes, nuclear tests.
Earthquake swarms: many small quakes for months without a major one.
Energy share: shallow 70–85%, intermediate 12–15%, deep 3–5%.
P-waves (compressional/pressure) travel at 5–8 km/s; S-waves are shear/distortional waves.
Charles F. Richter (1930s); moment magnitude scale is better for large quakes; Mercalli has 12 levels.
Largest recorded quake: 1960 Valdivia, Chile (9.4–9.6); 2004 Indian Ocean (9.1–9.3); 1950 Assam–Tibet (8.6); 2001 Gujarat (7.7).
Most of Andhra Pradesh lies in seismic Zones II and III.

items.title: Volcanoes — Types, Examples, Landforms & Volcanic Rock in India
items.body:
### Volcanoes in detail

**In one line**
Lava viscosity decides the volcano type — fluid basalt builds shields and flood basalts, sticky lava builds composite cones and lava domes, and huge eruptions leave calderas.

**The story**
A volcano is a vent through which magma, gases and ash reach the surface. Volcanoes are classed by activity as **active** (erupted in recent times — e.g. Barren Island), **dormant** (quiet but may erupt — e.g. Narcondam, Vesuvius was thought dormant before AD 79) and **extinct** (no eruption expected — e.g. Kilimanjaro is often cited as dormant/extinct). By form they fall into four main types.

| Type | Lava and shape | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Shield | very fluid, low-viscosity **basalt**; broad, gentle; the **largest** volcanoes; low explosivity (explosive only if water enters the vent); **short** intervals between eruptions | **Mauna Loa** and **Mauna Kea** (Hawaii), **Surtsey** (Iceland) |
| Composite (stratovolcano) | cooler, more viscous lava; layers of lava, ash and **tephra**; steep cones; **long** intervals; many on the Pacific Ring of Fire | **Mount St. Helens** (USA), **Vesuvius**, **Etna** (Italy), **Fuji** (Japan) |
| Caldera | collapse after a huge eruption empties the magma chamber; the **most explosive**; often fills with water | **Yellowstone** (USA), **Crater Lake** (Oregon) |
| Flood basalt | low-viscosity lava rich in iron and magnesium, low in silica; flows very far; also typical of **mid-ocean ridge** volcanism | **Deccan Traps** (most of the Maharashtra plateau) |

**Volcanic landforms**

| Landform | What it is |
|---|---|
| Volcanic cone | cone of lava, ash and pyroclastic debris |
| Crater | bowl-shaped depression at the summit |
| Caldera | enormous depression after collapse — a few to tens of km across |
| Lava dome | steep mound of **highly viscous** lava piled near the vent |
| Volcanic island | built up from the ocean floor by repeated eruptions |
| Volcanic neck | solidified magma of the conduit, exposed when the cone erodes |

**India's volcanic rock**
The **Deccan Traps** are a fissure (flood) basalt province; their weathering produced the **black cotton soil (regur)** — UPSC 2021 asked exactly this: black soil formed by the weathering of **fissure volcanic rock**. The world's highest volcano is **Ojos del Salado** (6,893 m, Chile–Argentina border).

**Terms explained**
- **Viscosity** — "thickness" of lava; high-silica lava is viscous and explosive, low-silica basalt is fluid.
- **Tephra** — fragments thrown out in an eruption (ash, cinders, bombs).

**Don't confuse**
Crater (summit bowl) vs caldera (huge collapse basin). Lava dome = viscous; shield = fluid.

**TL;DR**
- Shield: fluid basalt, largest, gentle (Mauna Loa, Mauna Kea, Surtsey).
- Composite: viscous, steep, layered (St. Helens, Vesuvius, Etna, Fuji).
- Caldera: most explosive collapse (Yellowstone, Crater Lake); flood basalt: Deccan Traps.
- Black cotton soil came from weathering of fissure volcanic rock (Deccan basalt); highest volcano Ojos del Salado.
keyPoints: Volcanoes by activity: active (Barren Island), dormant (Narcondam), extinct.
Shield volcanoes are the largest, of fluid basalt, with short intervals — Mauna Loa, Mauna Kea, Surtsey.
Composite (strato) volcanoes: viscous lava, tephra layers, long intervals — St. Helens, Vesuvius, Etna, Fuji.
Calderas are the most explosive — Yellowstone, Crater Lake (Oregon).
Flood basalt lava is rich in iron and magnesium and low in silica — Deccan Traps.
Lava domes form from highly viscous lava; volcanic necks are exposed solidified conduits.
Black cotton soil formed from weathering of fissure volcanic rock (UPSC 2021).
Ojos del Salado (6,893 m) is the highest volcano.

items.title: Rock-forming Minerals & the Three Rock Groups in Detail
items.body:
### Minerals and rocks in detail

**In one line**
A **rock** is an aggregate of one or more minerals; **feldspar** and **quartz** are the commonest; and each rock group has sub-types, examples and economic uses that exams pair up.

**The story**
The scientific study of rocks is **petrology**. Rocks are grouped by how they form into **igneous**, **sedimentary** and **metamorphic**.

**Rock-forming and ore minerals**

| Mineral | Key fact |
|---|---|
| Feldspar | about **half** the crust; light-coloured; silicon, oxygen, sodium, potassium, calcium, aluminium |
| Quartz | silicon + oxygen; **hexagonal** crystals; white/colourless, cracks like glass; in sand and granite; used in **radio and radar** |
| Bauxite | hydrous oxide of aluminium — the **ore of aluminium** |
| Cinnabar | the source of **mercury** |
| Dolomite | double carbonate of **calcium and magnesium**; used in cement and iron-and-steel |
| Gypsum | hydrous **calcium sulphate**; used in cement, fertiliser and chemicals |
| Haematite | the **red** ore of iron |
| Magnetite | the **black** ore of iron |
| Amphibole | about **7%** of the crust; used in the **asbestos** industry |
| Mica | about **4%** of the crust; in igneous and metamorphic rocks; used in **electrical** instruments |
| Olivine | magnesium, iron and silica; **greenish** crystals |
| Pyroxene | green or black; calcium, aluminium, magnesium, iron, silica |

**Igneous rocks** — formed by cooling of magma (below) or lava (above); called **primary** rocks; **un-fossiliferous** because they form at high temperature. By place of cooling:
- **Plutonic** — slow cooling at depth, large grains — **granite** (also gabbro).
- **Extrusive (volcanic)** — rapid cooling at the surface, fine grains — **basalt** (the Deccan Traps).
- **Dyke (intermediate)** — between the two, **semi-crystalline**.
By silica content they are **acidic** (silica-rich, e.g. granite) or **basic** (silica-poor, e.g. basalt). Igneous rocks yield magnetite, nickel, copper, chromite, gold, diamond and platinum; **amygdales** are gas bubbles in basalt later filled with minerals.

**Sedimentary rocks** — formed by **lithification** (compaction and consolidation of sediments); **stratified** (layered) and **fossiliferous**. Glacial deposits form **till/tillite**; wind deposits **loess**.

| Mode | Examples |
|---|---|
| Mechanically formed | sandstone, conglomerate, shale, loess — porous, the **best reservoirs** of groundwater and petroleum |
| Organically formed | coal, chalk, limestone, geyserite |
| Chemically formed | halite (rock salt), potash, limestone; **stalactites and stalagmites** |
Petroleum comes from the decay of tiny marine organisms in sedimentary rocks.

**Metamorphic rocks** — "change of form" by heat and pressure; minerals line up in layers called **foliation**. Causes: **orogenic movements**, **lava inflow**, and **geodynamic forces** (plate tectonics).

| Original | Agent | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Granite | pressure | gneiss |
| Clay/shale | pressure | schist |
| Clay/shale | heat | slate → phyllite |
| Sandstone | heat | quartzite |
| Coal | heat | anthracite → graphite |
| Limestone | heat | marble |

**Rock cycle** — igneous rocks are primary; their fragments form sedimentary rocks; both can become metamorphic; and **subduction** carries crustal rocks down to melt into magma again.

**Don't confuse**
Haematite = red iron ore; magnetite = black. Plutonic = granite (coarse); extrusive = basalt (fine).

**TL;DR**
- Feldspar ~half the crust; quartz in radio/radar; bauxite → aluminium; cinnabar → mercury; gypsum = calcium sulphate.
- Igneous: plutonic (granite), extrusive (basalt), dyke (semi-crystalline); acidic vs basic by silica; no fossils.
- Sedimentary: lithification, layered, fossils; mechanical/organic/chemical; sandstone is the best reservoir.
- Metamorphic: foliation; shale → slate → phyllite; coal → anthracite → graphite.
keyPoints: Petrology is the study of rocks; feldspar makes up about half the crust; quartz is used in radio and radar.
Bauxite is the ore of aluminium; cinnabar gives mercury; gypsum is hydrous calcium sulphate; dolomite is a Ca–Mg carbonate.
Haematite is the red ore and magnetite the black ore of iron.
Amphibole ~7% of the crust (asbestos); mica ~4% (electrical instruments).
Igneous rocks are primary and un-fossiliferous; plutonic (granite), extrusive (basalt), dyke (semi-crystalline).
Sedimentary rocks form by lithification and are stratified and fossiliferous; tillite = glacial, loess = wind.
Mechanically formed sedimentary rocks (sandstone) are the best reservoirs of groundwater and petroleum.
Foliation marks metamorphic rocks; shale → slate → phyllite; coal → anthracite → graphite.

items.title: Geological Time Scale — Full Table of Eras, Periods & Life
items.body:
### The geological calendar

**In one line**
The geological time scale arranges Earth's **4.6-billion-year** history into **eons, eras, periods and epochs**, each tagged by the life that appeared in it.

**The story**
An **eon** is the largest unit; it is divided into **eras**, eras into **periods**, and periods into **epochs**. Our source's figures (older textbook dates) are given below; the modern international chart differs slightly (for example the dinosaurs' end is now dated about **66 million years**, and the Cambrian start about **541 million years** ago).

| Era | Period / Epoch | Million years ago (source) | Life / event |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cainozoic | Quaternary – **Holocene** | 0 – 0.01 | **modern man** |
| | Quaternary – **Pleistocene** | 0.01 – 2 | **Homo sapiens** |
| | Tertiary – **Pliocene** | 2 – 5 | early human ancestors |
| | Tertiary – **Miocene** | 5 – 24 | flowering plants and trees |
| | Tertiary – **Oligocene** | 24 – 37 | **anthropoid apes** |
| | Tertiary – **Eocene** | 37 – 58 | rabbits and hares |
| | Tertiary – **Palaeocene** | 57 – 65 | small mammals (rats, mice) |
| Mesozoic | **Cretaceous** | 65 – 144 | **extinction of dinosaurs** |
| | **Jurassic** | 144 – 208 | **age of dinosaurs**; early birds |
| | **Triassic** | 208 – 245 | frogs and turtles |
| Palaeozoic | **Permian** | 245 – 286 | reptiles replace amphibians; ends in mass extinction |
| | **Carboniferous** | 286 – 360 | first reptiles; **coal beds** |
| | **Devonian** | 360 – 408 | **amphibians** |
| | **Silurian** | 408 – 438 | first life on land: **plants** |
| | **Ordovician** | 438 – 505 | **first fish** |
| | **Cambrian** | 505 – 570 | marine invertebrates; no land life |
| Pre-Cambrian | **Proterozoic** | 570 – 2,500 | soft-bodied arthropods |
| | **Archean** | 2,500 – 3,800 | **blue-green algae**, unicellular bacteria |
| | **Hadean** | 3,800 – 4,800 | oceans and continents form; CO₂-rich air |

Before that: origin of the Sun about 5,000 million years ago; Big Bang about 13,700 million years ago.

**Uses** — dating rocks and fossils, correlating rock strata across regions, **resource exploration** (oil, coal, minerals by rock age), past-climate studies, evolutionary biology and archaeology.
**Limitations** — an incomplete fossil record, assumptions about rates of change, dating-technique errors and conflicting interpretations (e.g. timing of mass extinctions).

**Don't confuse**
Jurassic = age of dinosaurs; Cretaceous = their extinction. Silurian = first land plants; Devonian = amphibians; Ordovician = first fish.

**TL;DR**
- Eon > Era > Period > Epoch; three later eras: Palaeozoic, Mesozoic, Cainozoic.
- Cambrian (no land life) → Ordovician (fish) → Silurian (land plants) → Devonian (amphibians) → Carboniferous (coal, first reptiles) → Permian.
- Triassic → Jurassic (dinosaurs) → Cretaceous (dinosaur extinction, ~65–66 mya).
- Oligocene apes; Pleistocene Homo sapiens; Holocene modern man (last 10,000 years); Archean blue-green algae.
keyPoints: Holocene (last 10,000 years) — modern man; Pleistocene — Homo sapiens; Oligocene — anthropoid apes.
Quaternary = Pleistocene + Holocene; Tertiary = Palaeocene to Pliocene.
Mesozoic: Triassic (frogs, turtles), Jurassic (age of dinosaurs), Cretaceous (dinosaur extinction).
Palaeozoic: Cambrian (marine invertebrates), Ordovician (first fish), Silurian (first land plants), Devonian (amphibians), Carboniferous (coal beds, first reptiles), Permian.
Archean — blue-green algae; Hadean — oceans and continents form with a CO2-rich atmosphere.
Modern chart: dinosaur extinction ~66 million years ago; Cambrian start ~541 million years ago.
Uses: dating, correlation of strata, resource exploration, climate studies; limitation: incomplete fossil record.

items.title: Geomorphic Processes — Endogenic Movements, Weathering Types & Erosion
items.body:
### How the surface is built up and worn down

**In one line**
**Geomorphology**, founded by **William Morris Davis**, studies landforms; endogenic movements (diastrophic and sudden) raise land, while exogenic **denudation** — weathering, mass wasting and erosion — lowers it.

**The story**
The energy behind endogenic movements is the Earth's **internal heat**, about **50%** of which comes from **radioactive decay**; temperature and pressure gradients create density differences and mantle **convection currents**. Endogenic movements are of two kinds:
- **Diastrophic** (slow, over thousands of years): **epeirogenic** movements act **radially** (along the Earth's radius) — continent-forming uplift and subsidence; **orogenic** movements act **tangentially** — mountain-building by folding and faulting at converging plates.
- **Sudden**: earthquakes and volcanoes at plate margins.

In short, **epeirogeny** is the broad, continent-wide uplift or warping of the crust, while **orogeny** is localised mountain-building by folding and faulting. An earthquake in **Chile (1822)** lifted the coast about 1 m; one in **New Zealand (1885)** up to 3 m.

Exogenic processes are driven by the **Sun's heat**; together weathering and erosion are called **denudation** ("denude" = to strip off). **Gravity** gives the direction to all downslope movement — without it no erosion would occur.

**Physical weathering**

| Process | How it works |
|---|---|
| Exfoliation by **unloading** | removal of overlying rock releases pressure; upper layers expand and peel in sheets |
| Exfoliation by **thermal stress** | daily heating/cooling peels surface layers; strongest in **dry climates and high elevations** |
| **Granular disintegration** | dark minerals absorb more heat than light ones, so grains loosen one by one |
| **Frost weathering** | ice grows in cracks — frost shattering, **frost-wedging**, freeze–thaw |
| **Salt weathering** | salt crystals grow in pores — typical of **arid** climates |

**Chemical weathering**

| Process | How it works |
|---|---|
| Dissolution / solution | soluble minerals (nitrates, sulphates) dissolve; acidic water dissolves more |
| **Carbonation** | rain + CO₂ = weak **carbonic acid**, which turns limestone into soluble **calcium bicarbonate** — makes caves and **karst** |
| **Hydration** | minerals take up water and swell (iron oxide → larger iron hydroxide) |
| Hydrolysis | water reacts with silicate or carbonate minerals, dissolving them |
| Oxidation / reduction | reaction with oxygen (rusting of iron minerals) |

**Biological weathering** — lichens and mosses, plant roots in crevices, burrowing earthworms and rodents, and acids from decaying matter.
**Significance** — weathering is the **first step in soil formation**, enriches some ores by leaching, and makes resources easier to exploit.

**Mass wasting** — downslope movement of soil and rock under **gravity** when the pull exceeds the slope's resistance (landslides).

**Erosion by water**

| Type | Feature |
|---|---|
| Raindrop (splash) | raindrops act like tiny bombs; vegetation prevents it |
| Sheet | thin layer of soil washed off evenly |
| Rill → gully | finger-like rills enlarge into gullies — the **Chambal ravines** and the **Chos of Hoshiarpur** (Punjab) |
| Streambank, coastal, glacial | river banks, storm surges/tidal bores, moving glaciers |

**Erosion by wind** — fine and medium sand moves in leaps (**saltation**), dust travels far in **suspension**, coarse sand rolls (**surface creep**); coarse fragments left behind form **desert pavement**; wind-scoured depressions reaching groundwater become **oases**.

**Don't confuse**
Epeirogenic = radial, broad; orogenic = tangential, mountain-building. Weathering + erosion = denudation (aggradation is the building-up side).

**TL;DR**
- W. M. Davis founded geomorphology; ~50% of internal heat is from radioactive decay.
- Epeirogenic (radial) vs orogenic (tangential); sudden movements: earthquakes and volcanoes.
- Physical weathering: exfoliation, granular disintegration, frost, salt; chemical: carbonation, hydration, hydrolysis, oxidation.
- Gully erosion: Chambal ravines; wind moves sand by saltation, suspension and surface creep.
keyPoints: William Morris Davis (1850–1934) founded geomorphology.
About 50% of Earth's internal heat comes from radioactive decay.
Epeirogenic movements are radial (continent-forming); orogenic movements are tangential (mountain-building).
Denudation = weathering + erosion, driven by solar energy; gravity directs all downslope movement.
Thermal-stress exfoliation is strongest in dry climates and high elevations; salt weathering in arid climates.
Carbonation: carbonic acid turns limestone into calcium bicarbonate, forming caves and karst.
Weathering is the first step in soil formation.
Gully erosion: Chambal ravines and the Chos of Hoshiarpur; wind moves sand by saltation, suspension and surface creep; desert pavement remains.

items.title: River Landforms in Detail — Processes, Stages, Waterfalls & Delta Types
items.body:
### What a river carves and builds

**In one line**
A river erodes by hydraulic action, corrosion, abrasion and attrition, cuts **V-valleys** and **gorges** when young, **meanders** when mature, and builds **deltas** of many shapes in old age.

**The story**
**Fluvial erosion** works in several ways: **hydraulic action** (the sheer force of water — our source calls it "hydration"), **corrosion** (chemical action), **abrasion** (load scraping the bed and banks) and **attrition** (load particles colliding and breaking each other). Erosion acts **downward** (downcutting deepens the valley), **sideways** (lateral erosion widens it) and **headward** (the source retreats upstream, lengthening the channel). Where slope is low and load is heavy the channel splits around **braid bars** — **braiding**.

**Stages of a river**

| Stage | Features | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Youth | fast, steep **V-shaped valleys**, **gorges**, waterfalls, rapids; vertical erosion | Himalayan rivers (gorges over 500 m deep) |
| Maturity | lateral erosion; valley floor widens; **meanders** in soft alluvium | rivers of the Indo-Gangetic–Brahmaputra plain |
| Old age | deposition, river islands, braiding, **deltas** | **Majuli** (Brahmaputra, Assam) — world's largest river island; Ganga–Brahmaputra delta |

A **canyon** is an extended gorge — the **Grand Canyon** of the **Colorado River** (Arizona) is **483 km** long and **2.88 km** deep. A **tributary (hanging) valley** joins the main valley over a steep step, often as a waterfall.

**Erosional features**
- **Waterfalls** form from differences in rock resistance, relief, falls in sea level (rejuvenation) and earth movements. **Kunchikal Falls** (Varahi river, Shimoga, Karnataka; **455 m**, a cascade) is India's highest; **Jog (Gersoppa) Falls** (**253 m**, Sharavathi river) is the famous plunge fall; **Angel Falls** (Venezuela, **979 m**) is the world's highest.
- **Potholes** — cylindrical holes drilled into the rocky bed by stones swirling in eddies.
- **River terraces** — stepped benches marking former valley floors.
- **Meanders** — the outer bank (**cliff-slope**, concave) erodes; the inner bank (**slip-off slope**, convex) gets deposits.
- **Oxbow lakes** — cut-off meanders that turn into swamps. The southward shift of the Ganga left many north of its course; **Kanwar Lake** (Begusarai, Bihar) is the largest oxbow lake in India/Asia (our source calls it Bihar's only Ramsar site — Bihar has since added more).
- **Peneplain** — an almost flat plain with low residual hills, the end product of the erosion cycle.

**Depositional features**
- **Alluvial fans/cones** — where streams leave mountains (Himalayan foothills).
- **Natural levees** — low ridges along banks; a breach floods the land (Hwang Ho, China).
- **Delta** — forms because the river slows on entering the sea and **clay coagulates in salt water**; the finest particles settle farthest as **bottom-set beds**.

| Delta type | Feature | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Arcuate | fan-shaped, convex to the sea | **Nile**, **Ganga** |
| Bird's-foot | claw-shaped; river stronger than waves | **Mississippi** |
| Cuspate | tooth-shaped; strong waves on a straight coast | **Tiber** (Italy) |
| Estuarine | in submerged river mouths | **Seine**, **Narmada and Tapi** |
| Lacustrine | river entering a lake | Lough Leane (Ireland) |
| Truncated | cut back by waves and currents | — |
| Abandoned | river shifts its mouth | **Yellow River**; western Ganga delta (Hooghly) |

**Why the Narmada flows west (UPSC 2013)** — it occupies a linear **rift valley** (between the Vindhya and Satpura blocks) and the land slopes to the west from Central India.

**Don't confuse**
Cliff-slope (outer, eroding) vs slip-off slope (inner, depositing). Narmada and Tapi make estuaries, not true deltas.

**TL;DR**
- Processes: hydraulic action, corrosion, abrasion, attrition; downcutting, lateral, headward erosion; braiding.
- Youth V-valley/gorge → maturity meanders → old age delta; Majuli is the largest river island.
- Grand Canyon 483 km long, 2.88 km deep; Kunchikal 455 m, Jog 253 m, Angel 979 m.
- Deltas: arcuate (Nile, Ganga), bird's-foot (Mississippi), cuspate (Tiber), estuarine (Narmada, Tapi), abandoned (Yellow River).
keyPoints: Fluvial erosion: hydraulic action, corrosion, abrasion, attrition; downcutting, lateral and headward erosion.
Braided channels split around braid bars where slope is low and sediment load high.
Grand Canyon of the Colorado: 483 km long, 2.88 km deep; Himalayan gorges exceed 500 m.
Majuli (Brahmaputra, Assam) is the world's largest river island.
Kunchikal Falls (Varahi, 455 m) is India's highest; Jog/Gersoppa (Sharavathi, 253 m); Angel Falls (979 m) is the world's highest.
Meanders: outer cliff-slope (concave, eroding) and inner slip-off slope (convex, depositing).
Kanwar Lake (Begusarai, Bihar) is the largest oxbow lake in India/Asia.
Peneplain is the end product of the erosion cycle.
Deltas form as river speed falls and clay coagulates in salt water; delta types: arcuate, bird's-foot, cuspate, estuarine, lacustrine, truncated, abandoned.

items.title: Glaciers & Deserts in Detail — Glacier Types, Snowline, Arid Landforms & Dunes
items.body:
### Ice and wind at work

**In one line**
Glaciers (moving ice, a few metres a day) come in four types and leave a long list of erosional and depositional forms; deserts add bolsons, pediments, bajadas, dunes and loess.

**The story — glaciers**
A **glacier** is a mass of ice moving at a few metres a day, armed with rock debris that grinds the land.

| Glacier type | Where |
|---|---|
| Continental (ice sheet) | **Antarctica** and **Greenland** (our source wrongly names Iceland as the biggest — Antarctica's is the largest) |
| Ice cap | snow-and-ice covers on mountains that feed valley glaciers |
| Piedmont | continuous ice sheet at the foot of mountains — **southern Alaska** |
| Valley (Alpine) | high mountains such as the Himalayas |

India's largest glacier is **Siachen** in the **Karakoram** (about **72 km**; often given as ~76 km); **Gangotri** (about **25.5 km**) is in **Uttarakhand** (source says Uttar Pradesh — the old undivided state).

**More glacial forms**
- **Glacial trough** — a stream valley reshaped into a **U-shape** by uniform glacial erosion.
- **Hanging valley** — a small tributary glacier's valley left high above the main valley (discordant tributary).
- **Horn** — a pyramid peak cut from **more than two sides** (an **arete** is cut from two sides).
- **Outwash (till) plain** — stratified debris left where the glacier melts.
- **Kame terraces** — sediment collected in ponds between ice and the valley side.
- **Drumlin** — an **inverted-boat**-shaped mound on the till plain.
- **Kettle hole** — a basin where deposits sag (often holding a lake).
- **Esker** — embankment-like ridge often used for **roads**.
- **Moraine** — debris carried by a glacier: **ground** moraine (beneath) and **end** (terminal) moraine; also lateral and medial.

**Why the highest mountains lie near the equator**
Mountains rise only about **1,500 m above their snowline**, because cold-climate glacial erosion cuts them down. Near the equator the snowline is high (about **5,500 m**), so peaks reach about **7,000 m**; in Canada or Chile the snowline is about 1,000 m, so peaks reach only about 2.5 km.

**The story — arid lands**

| Landform | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Bolson | intermontane basin in a dry region |
| Playa | temporary lake in a bolson |
| Pediment | **erosional** rock-cut surface at a mountain foot (an alluvial fan looks similar but is **depositional**) |
| Bajada | gentle depositional plain formed by **coalescing alluvial fans**, between pediment and playa |
| Deflation basin (blowout) | hollow scooped by wind |
| Mushroom rock (pedestal rock) | rock undercut near its base |
| Inselberg (monadnock) | isolated hill rising abruptly from a plain (e.g. Uluru) |
| Demoiselle | rock pillar of hard rock capping soft rock |
| Zeugen | **table-shaped** ridge of hard rock over soft rock |
| Wind window / bridge | hole abraded through rock, widened into an arch |
| Ripple marks | small depositional ridges made by **saltation** |

**Sand dunes** (a few metres to 20 m high, some several hundred metres):

| Dune | Shape |
|---|---|
| Barchan | crescent, tips **downwind** |
| Transverse | long straight ridges **perpendicular** to the wind |
| Seif | long **linear** dunes in parallel rows |
| Star | arms radiating from a centre — winds from **many directions** |
| Parabolic | U-shaped, tips **upwind**, held by vegetation |

**Loess** — fertile wind-blown silt at desert edges: northern China (**Yellow River**, the Loess/Huangtu Plateau), the Great Plains of North America (thickest near the **Missouri River, Iowa**), central Europe, Russia and Kazakhstan.

**Desert types** — all get under about **250 mm** of rain a year: **subtropical/hot** (Sahara, Arabian, Kalahari), **cold** (Gobi, Great Basin, Atacama), **coastal** (Namib, Peruvian — cold currents and fog) and **rain-shadow** (Mojave, Patagonia). The largest deserts are the polar **Antarctic** (about 14.2 million km²) and **Arctic**.

**Don't confuse**
Barchan tips downwind; parabolic tips upwind. Pediment = erosional; bajada = depositional. Arete = two sides; horn = more than two.

**TL;DR**
- Glacier types: continental (Antarctica, Greenland), ice cap, piedmont (Alaska), valley; Siachen ~72 km, Gangotri ~25.5 km.
- Drumlin = inverted boat; kettle = basin; kame terrace; moraine ground/end; equator snowline ~5,500 m.
- Arid: bolson, playa, pediment (erosional), bajada (fans), zeugen (table), yardang, inselberg, demoiselle.
- Dunes: barchan, transverse, seif, star, parabolic; loess in China and Iowa; deserts get < 250 mm.
keyPoints: Glacier types: continental (Antarctica, Greenland), ice caps, piedmont (southern Alaska), valley/Alpine (Himalayas).
Siachen (Karakoram, ~72 km) is India's largest glacier; Gangotri is ~25.5 km.
Horn is cut from more than two sides; drumlin is inverted-boat-shaped; kettle holes are basins; eskers are used for roads.
Moraines: ground and end (terminal); kame terraces form between ice and valley side.
Mountains rise ~1,500 m above the snowline; equatorial snowline ~5,500 m.
Pediment is erosional; bajada is formed by coalescing alluvial fans; playa is a temporary lake in a bolson.
Zeugen are table-shaped; demoiselles are rock pillars; inselberg = monadnock.
Dunes: barchan (tips downwind), transverse (perpendicular), seif (linear), star (many winds), parabolic (tips upwind, vegetation).
Loess: Yellow River/Loess Plateau, Great Plains (Missouri River, Iowa); deserts receive under 250 mm of rain.

items.title: Karst & Coastal Landforms in Detail — with India & AP Examples
items.body:
### Limestone country and the coast

**In one line**
Karst scenery comes from **carbonic acid** dissolving limestone and dolomite, giving sinkholes, uvalas, poljes and caves; the sea cuts platforms, arches and stacks and builds bars, spits, lagoons and tombolos.

**The story — karst**
Pure limestone is **calcium carbonate**; with magnesium it is **dolomite**. Rain picks up CO₂ from the air and soil and becomes weak **carbonic acid**, which dissolves the rock. Karst areas have little surface drainage — water flows **underground**. The name comes from the **Karst (Kras) region** of former **Yugoslavia** on the **Adriatic** coast (now Slovenia).

| Karst form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Sinkhole / swallow hole | funnel-shaped hollow; surface streams vanish down **swallow holes** |
| Doline | small solution depression |
| Uvala | long trench formed by joined dolines |
| Polje | large **U-shaped** valley from coalescing uvalas |
| Blind valley | a valley in which the stream disappears |
| Cave / tunnel | dissolved along bedding planes; a cave open at both ends is a **tunnel** |
| Stalactite | hangs from the ceiling, broad base tapering down |
| Stalagmite | rises from the floor |
| Column / pillar | stalactite and stalagmite joined |
| Sinking creek / boga | stream lost through cracks; open-topped ones are **bogas** |

**Caves in India** — **Bastar** (Kotumsar, Chhattisgarh), **Dehradun** and the **Shillong plateau** (Meghalaya, home to India's longest caves). **AP angle:** **Borra Caves** in the **Ananthagiri hills** (Visakhapatnam region) and **Belum Caves** (Kurnool region) — the **second-largest** cave system in India and the longest open to the public in the plains.

**The story — the coast**
Waves compress air in cracks, hurl debris against the rock, and chemically attack limestone and chalk.

| Erosional | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Chasm | narrow deep notch cut along weak planes; widens into a **bay** |
| Wave-cut platform | flat rock bench left as the cliff retreats; a **notch** forms at the cliff foot |
| Sea cave → sea arch → stack | differential erosion; when an arch collapses the pillar left is a **stack** (skerry / chimney rock) |
| Hanging valley | stream valley left hanging above a retreating coast |

| Depositional | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Beach | temporary cover of debris on a wave-cut platform |
| Bar | submerged ridge of sand offshore; water behind it becomes a **lagoon** |
| Barrier | the **above-water** counterpart of a bar |
| Spit / hook | sand ridge joined to land at one end; a short curved spit is a **hook** |
| Tombolo | bar linking an island to the mainland or another island |

**Coast types** — a **ria coast** forms when river valleys are drowned (**south-west Ireland**); a **fjord coast** when glacial troughs are drowned (**Norway**). India's **west coast** is largely **submergent** (narrow, with estuaries); the **east coast** is **emergent** (broad plains, deltas, lagoons). **AP angle:** **Pulicat Lake** on the AP–Tamil Nadu border is a lagoon behind the **Sriharikota** barrier island — India's second-largest brackish lagoon after **Chilika** (Odisha).

**Don't confuse**
Stalactite (ceiling, "c") vs stalagmite (ground, "g"). Bar is submerged; barrier stands above water. Ria = drowned river valley; fjord = drowned glacial valley.

**TL;DR**
- Karst: carbonic acid on limestone/dolomite; named after Karst (Yugoslavia, Adriatic); doline → uvala → polje.
- Caves: Bastar, Dehradun, Shillong plateau; AP: Borra (Ananthagiri) and Belum (second-largest in India).
- Coast: chasm, wave-cut platform + notch, cave → arch → stack; bar, barrier, spit, hook, tombolo, lagoon.
- Ria (SW Ireland) vs fjord (Norway); Pulicat lagoon lies behind Sriharikota island.
keyPoints: Karst is named after the Karst region of former Yugoslavia on the Adriatic coast; limestone = calcium carbonate, dolomite contains magnesium.
Dolines join to form uvalas; uvalas coalesce into U-shaped poljes; streams vanish in blind valleys and swallow holes.
A cave open at both ends is a tunnel; sinking creeks with open tops are bogas.
Caves in India: Bastar, Dehradun, Shillong plateau; AP: Borra Caves (Ananthagiri hills) and Belum Caves (second-largest in India).
Wave-cut platform with a notch at the cliff foot; sea arch collapses to leave a stack (skerry/chimney rock).
A bar is submerged, a barrier stands above water; a short curved spit is a hook; a tombolo links islands.
Ria coast: south-west Ireland; fjord coast: Norway.
India's west coast is submergent, the east coast emergent; Pulicat lagoon lies behind Sriharikota island.
